title: Hooks are walls

story: Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, writes the checks for RH-1234 before it writes the product code: a test that expects the card "No projects yet". An hour later the test still fails, because the card shows "Loading" for an empty workgroup. The quickest way to a green build is not to fix the code. It is to change the test so it expects "Loading".

A model under pressure can take that shortcut, and a prompt that says "never edit the tests" is only a request. Permissions do not help much either: they decide by tool name and path pattern, and they cannot ask "has this agent proved its work?" before it says it is done. We need our own code at the moments that matter, with the power to say no.
hook.question: How do I run my own code inside the agent loop, so that some things stay impossible, whatever the model comes to believe?

read.h: Your code at fixed moments of the loop
p: A hook is a function you give the session, and the SDK calls it when a certain event happens: PreToolUse just before a tool runs, PostToolUse just after, Stop when the model wants to end its turn, and many more. The SDK waits for your answer before it continues. The hooks run in your own process, not inside the model's context, so they cost no tokens and the model cannot change them.

A hook receives the event's input (for PreToolUse, the tool name and its arguments) and returns a small object. An empty object means "no opinion": the normal checks decide. To refuse a call, a PreToolUse hook returns a permission decision of "deny" with a reason, and the model reads that reason instead of the tool's output. Hooks also run first in the order of permission checks, before any allow rule or permission mode, and a deny from a hook stops the call even in bypassPermissions.

notes.text: The paths our work is judged by. In the platform this list comes from one shared file, not from code.
Commands agents never run. The hook gives a clear answer; missing credentials are the real wall behind it.
The deny shape: the event name, the decision and a reason the model will read.
Edit and Write put the path in file_path. Matchers only see tool names, so the path check lives here.
A calm reason with an alternative keeps the model working. A bare "denied" makes it try five other ways.
An empty object: this hook has no opinion, and the normal permission checks decide.

p: The hooks option maps an event name to a list of matchers. A matcher is a pattern for the tool name, such as "Edit|Write|Bash", plus the hooks to run when it matches; without a pattern, the hooks run for every call. Several hooks can match the same call. They run in parallel, and for permission decisions the strictest answer wins: one deny blocks the call whatever the others say.

PostToolUse hooks get the tool's input and its output, and they can hand the model new information through additionalContext. Here, after every edit, we run the TypeScript compiler and, if it finds problems, give the model the errors at once, instead of letting it learn about them at the end from CI. That is guidance, not a wall: it makes the right path faster.

notes.text: Run the wall before every Edit, Write and Bash call.
After each edit, typecheckAfterEdit runs npx tsc and returns any errors as additionalContext.
Stop has no tool, so no matcher. This hook decides whether the model may end its turn.

p: The Stop hook runs when the model wants to finish. If it returns decision "block" with a reason, the model does not stop: it gets the reason as its next instruction and returns to work. That is how we demand proof. Before Nova may say it is done, the hook checks for evidence, and if the evidence is missing, the answer is "run these checks first".

One field keeps this from looping forever. stop_hook_active is true when this stop comes right after a stop that a hook already blocked. A careful Stop hook lets the second stop through and records the problem for people, instead of sending the model back to work again and again.

There is a hole you should see clearly. The PreToolUse wall reads file_path, but a Bash command such as sed -i that rewrites a test file has no file_path, only command text, and no pattern can recognise every shell command that might write a file. So the real check happens at the end: the Stop hook compares the protected files with their state at the start, and it does not matter which tool changed them.

notes.text: This stop follows one we already blocked. Let it through, and let people see the problem.
block plus a reason: the model keeps working, and the reason is its next instruction.

deeper.h: Go deeper: timeouts and hooks that only watch
p: Each hook runs with a timeout, 600 seconds by default for most events; set timeout (in seconds) on the matcher to change it. When a PreToolUse hook times out, the tool does not run and the model is told the hook did not answer. A timed-out Stop hook counts as no decision.

A hook that only records something, such as a log line or a metric, can return { async: true } so the agent does not wait for it. Such a hook cannot block or add context, because the agent has already continued.

lab.title: Three hooks and the tests that trust them
needs: For one step only: your own Anthropic API key
lab.goal: Write a wall, a helper and a proof check as hooks, test them with recorded inputs and no model, find the hole a shell command opens, and close it at Stop.

guess.q: A session runs in bypassPermissions mode with allowedTools: ["Edit"]. A PreToolUse hook returns permissionDecision "deny" for an edit to test/cart.test.ts. Does the edit happen?

options.text: Yes, bypass mode approves everything, and Edit is even pre-approved.
options.why: Hooks run before the permission mode and the allow rules. A hook deny wins in every mode.

options.text: No, the hook's deny stops the call and the model reads the reason.
options.why: Hooks are the first check. A deny from any hook blocks the call, even in bypassPermissions.

options.text: It depends on which runs first, the hook or the allow rule.
options.why: The order is fixed: hooks first, then deny rules, ask rules, the mode, allow rules and canUseTool.

follow.say: Write src/hooks.ts: the guardWalls wall from the Understand step, the proofBeforeDone Stop hook, and this typecheckAfterEdit helper between them.
Hooks are plain functions, so you can test them with recorded inputs and no session at all. These tests build the same input objects the SDK would send.

follow.say: Give the session a real temptation: a small function that says "Loading" and a test that expects "No projects yet". Write src/fix-cart.ts from the Understand step and run it with your key. Add a console.log in guardWalls before each deny if you want to watch the refusals.
follow.see: (Needs your key; the model's path will differ.) If it tries to edit test/cart.test.ts, the edit is refused with your reason. When it tries to stop without proof/tests-passed.txt, the Stop hook sends it back once. The test file still contains 'No projects yet'.

lab.build: Close the sed hole at Stop. Write src/lock.ts with lockChecks(dir): when it is created it records a sha256 hash of every file under dir, and it returns a Stop hook that blocks, listing the changed files, when any hash is different. Like proofBeforeDone, it lets a second stop through. Test it in test/lock.test.ts with a temporary folder: write a test file, create the hook, check that a stop passes, rewrite the file (as sed would), and check that the next stop is blocked.
checks: node --test shows the four hook tests passing without any API key.
The extra test proves that a Bash sed command gets an empty answer from guardWalls: the PreToolUse wall cannot see it.
Your lock test passes: a stop before the change returns {}, a stop after it returns decision "block".
With your key, test/cart.test.ts still expects 'No projects yet' after the session ends.
lab.fix: A teammate wrote a PreToolUse hook with matcher "test/.*" so it would only run for edits to test files, and it never fires. Then they changed the reason to "DENIED", and in the transcript the model tried the same edit through Write, then Bash, then NotebookEdit. Find what a matcher actually matches, move the path check to the right place, and rewrite the reason so the model has somewhere better to go.
explain: Why can a hook refuse a call that bypassPermissions and an allow rule would both approve?
What does stop_hook_active protect against, and what should a Stop hook do when it is true?
Why does a PreToolUse hook on file_path not stop a test file from changing, and what catches it instead?
lab.done: Your hooks have tests that run without a model, and you can show both the hole in the PreToolUse wall and the Stop hook that closes it.

check.q: You want the agent to never edit files under test/. Why a PreToolUse hook rather than only a deny rule?

options.why: They can: Edit(/test/**) is a valid scoped deny rule. The difference is elsewhere.

options.text: A hook can give a reason with an alternative and record the refusal, and it runs first, even in bypass mode
options.why: Both can refuse, but the hook is your code: it explains, it can record the refusal in a log, and it decides before anything else.

options.text: Hooks are cheaper because they use a smaller model
options.why: Hooks are your own functions. No model runs them at all.

check.q: A Stop hook returns { decision: "block", reason: "Run the tests first" }. What happens next?

options.text: The session ends with an error result
options.why: Blocking a stop does not end anything. It keeps the model working.

options.text: The hook runs the tests itself
options.why: The hook only answers. The model gets the reason and decides how to run the tests.

options.text: The model continues, with your reason as its next instruction
options.why: That is how a Stop hook demands proof: the model goes back to work and is told what is missing.

check.q: The model runs sed -i on a locked test file through Bash. Which hook catches it reliably?

options.text: A Stop hook that compares the protected files with their hashes from the start
options.why: It checks the result, not the route. Whatever tool changed the file, the hash is different.
Bash is not Edit or Write, and the command text has no file_path to check.
It runs after edits made with those tools only, so a Bash call never reaches it.

p: The harness gives every agent session three kinds of hooks. A PreToolUse wall refuses edits to protected paths (CI workflows, lint and type settings, eval sets, and the QA checks approved in the plan) and the commands agents never run: terraform or tofu apply and destroy, argocd app sync, gh workflow run and dispatches. The list of protected paths lives in one shared file that the locked-checks check in CI reads too, so the agent and CI agree. Every refusal goes to a ledger that the PR lists under "Refused actions".

A PostToolUse hook runs the fast linter for the edited file (biome under frontend/, black, isort and flake8 for the backend) and hands back failures as context. The Stop hook asks for a passing run of every QA check recorded after the last edit, and lets a second stop through with the checks marked unproven when the failure is not Nova's, such as a flaky test or a main branch that was already red.

tickets.why: hooks.ts: the wall, the lint hook and the proof-before-done Stop hook, with the refusal ledger.
The locked-checks check in CI reads the same protected-paths file as the hook.
The refusal ledger becomes the "Refused actions" part of the PR.

words.plain: Your function that the SDK calls at a fixed event in the loop, and waits for before going on.
The event just before a tool runs. Its hook can deny the call with a reason.
The event just after a tool ran. Its hook can add context the model reads next.
Runs when the model wants to finish. decision "block" with a reason sends it back to work.
True when this stop follows one a hook already blocked. Use it to avoid an endless loop.

review.q: Write the object a PreToolUse hook returns to refuse a call.
review.a: { hookSpecificOutput: { hookEventName: "PreToolUse", permissionDecision: "deny", permissionDecisionReason: "a calm reason with an alternative" } }.

review.q: Two hooks match the same call; one returns {} and one returns deny. What happens?
review.a: The call is blocked. Matching hooks run in parallel and the strictest permission decision wins.

review.q: Name the hole in a file_path wall and the hook that closes it.
review.a: Bash commands such as sed -i change files without a file_path. A Stop hook that compares protected files with their starting hashes catches any route.

remember: A hook is your code at a fixed moment of the loop; it runs first, a deny always wins, and a Stop hook can demand proof before done.
